title: Single-Hop HRA-Secure Owner-Encrypted Lattice-Based Proxy Re-Encryption without Statistical Noise Flooding
authors: Haotian Yin, Jie Zhang, Yuji Dong, Dominik Wojtczak, and Eng Gee Lim
abstract:
Existing lattice-based proxy re-encryption (PRE) schemes that achieve security against honest re-encryption attacks (HRA) typically rely on statistical noise flooding to hide dependencies between the source ciphertext, the re-encryption key, and the re-encrypted ciphertext. While effective, this technique causes large noise growth and significant parameter expansion.

We present an owner-encrypted proxy re-encryption (OE-PRE) construction that achieves single-hop HRA security without statistical noise flooding. In the owner-encrypted setting, ciphertexts are generated directly using the data owner's secret key, yielding a clean inherited-noise term during re-encryption. 

To formalise the leakage argument, we use noisy error-leakage LWE (NEL-LWE), which captures LWE hardness in the presence of a noisy observation of the error and follows from a special case of the Leaky-LWE framework of Lai, Swarnakar, and Woo (CiC 2025). 
We prove single-hop HRA security from standard LWE/RLWE-style pseudorandomness assumptions, the NEL-LWE consequence of Leaky-LWE, and PRF security via a direct HRA hybrid proof.
Our parameter discussion shows that the HRA-specific computational padding remains at the same scale as the encryption error, in contrast to the large flooding widths required in prior HRA-secure lattice PRE schemes. The proposed scheme targets single-hop owner-generated access delegation, such as encrypted file sharing and publish/subscribe delivery.

1     Introduction

Proxy re-encryption (PRE), introduced by Blaze, Bleumer, and Strauss [BBS98],
enables a semi-trusted proxy to transform a ciphertext encrypted for one user
into a ciphertext decryptable by another user, without revealing the underlying
plaintext.
    Lattice-based PRE has attracted significant attention due to its post-quantum
security and its natural compatibility with key-switching techniques. In such
schemes, re-encryption typically transforms a ciphertext by approximately evalu-
ating the source-key decryption relation and re-encoding the result under the tar-
get key. As a consequence, the re-encrypted ciphertext may retain residual noise
inherited from the source ciphertext, together with additional key-switching
noise. This residual noise can become visible through honest re-encryption tran-
scripts and may leak information correlated with the source secret key, even
when the underlying encryption scheme is IND-CPA-secure.
    Cohen [Coh19] formalised this phenomenon by showing that IND-CPA secu-
rity alone is insufficient for PRE. An adversary may obtain honestly re-encrypted
ciphertexts and exploit information leaked through the re-encryption procedure.
Existing lattice-based HRA-secure PRE constructions address this issue using
statistical noise flooding: the proxy adds a large fresh Gaussian error during
re-encryption, so that the resulting ciphertext becomes statistically independent
of the original re-encryption randomness. This statistical hiding is then used to
establish re-encryption simulatability and, consequently, HRA security.
    While effective, this approach comes at a high cost. The added masking
noise must statistically dominate the pre-existing error terms, often requiring a
variance substantially larger than that of the underlying encryption noise. As a
result, re-encryption consumes a significant portion of the available noise budget
and forces larger correctness parameters. Although FHE-style noise-management
tools such as modulus switching or bootstrapping can be used to support further
re-encryptions, they introduce additional parameters and computational costs.
In the absence of such tools, statistical flooding directly reduces the number of
feasible re-encryption hops. This dependence on statistical domination raises a
natural question:

      Can HRA security be achieved through computational masking of the
      inherited ciphertext noise?


1.1    Our Results

In this work, we answer this question affirmatively in the owner-encrypted single-
hop setting. We show that, when ciphertexts are generated directly by the data
owner, the inherited encryption noise has a clean enough form to be protected
by computational leakage masking rather than by statistical domination.
    The proposed scheme targets the single-hop owner-generated access-delegation
layer that appears in encrypted file-sharing/storage systems and publish/subscribe
                        Single-Hop HRA-Secure OE-PRE without Flooding           3

delivery. In these settings, a data owner or publisher generates an encrypted ob-
ject and a semi-trusted storage server or broker later transforms it once for an
authorised recipient [AFGH06, PRSV17]. We give a detailed discussion of the
application scope and limitations in Section 5.
    Our contributions are as follows.

 – We propose a BGV-style owner-encrypted proxy re-encryption (OE-PRE)
   construction. Re-encryption remains unidirectional and uses Alice’s secret
   key together with Bob’s public key to generate the re-encryption key. The
   owner-encrypted form yields a simple inherited-noise term, which is the basis
   of our leakage-masking argument.
 – We use noisy error-leakage LWE (NEL-LWE) to capture the hardness of
   distinguishing LWE samples in the presence of noisy error leakage. The NEL-
   LWE condition needed in our proof follows from the recent Leaky-LWE
   framework of Lai, Swarnakar, and Woo [LSW25] in the error-only leakage
   setting.
 – We prove single-hop HRA security directly inside the HRA game. The proof
   preserves the algebraic consistency of visible honest-to-honest re-encryption
   transcripts, while showing that honest-to-corrupted re-encryption responses
   reveal only computationally harmless noisy error leakage.

    Our model is a stateful-proxy OE-PRE model: the proxy keeps a private PRF
key κpad used only to derive deterministic per-ciphertext padding. The HRA ad-
versary may obtain admissible re-encryption keys and re-encryption transcripts,
but it is not given the proxy’s private padding state.
    Overall, our work shows that the single-hop owner-generated access-delegation
layer of lattice-based PRE can be protected by computational leakage masking
while remaining reducible to standard LWE-style assumptions.


1.2   Technical Overview

The key idea is to replace statistical domination of the inherited ciphertext
noise by computational leakage masking. In flooding-based HRA proofs, the re-
encryption noise is chosen large enough to statistically erase the dependence on
the incoming ciphertext and re-encryption randomness. In our construction, the
proxy instead exposes only a padded version of the owner-encryption error and
proves that this leakage is computationally harmless. The tool for this step is
NEL-LWE, which follows from the Leaky-LWE framework under the parameter
conditions stated in Corollary 1.
    The owner-encrypted setting is crucial. A standard public-key LWE cipher-
text contains inherited noise of the form epk v + se1 + e0 , which is a correlated
convolution of several random sources and does not directly match the error-
leakage form needed in our proof. By contrast, an owner-generated ciphertext
under Alice’s secret key sA satisfies

where ect is a fresh encryption error. This clean inherited error is the quantity
protected by our leakage argument.
    During re-encryption, the proxy performs BGV-style key switching from sA
to Bob’s key and adds a deterministic padding value epad (ct) derived from a
proxy-held PRF key and the source ciphertext encoding. The padding is fixed
for each source ciphertext, a method used in recent threshold encryption [MS25,
OT26]. This prevents an adversary from obtaining many independent masked
versions of the same error and averaging them to recover information about ect .
For honest-to-corrupted re-encryption queries, the exposed legacy term has the
form
                                 ect + epad (ct),
which is exactly the noisy error-leakage pattern that NEL-LWE handles.
     Fixed padding must also be protected in visible, honest-to-honest transcripts.
If it were added in the clear, a visible re-encryption key and its matching output
would allow public subtraction of pepad (ct). We therefore add a fresh target-key
zero-encryption shield Cfr to every re-encryption. After subtracting the visible
key-switching contribution, the adversary sees a BGV encryption-form sample
with offset pepad under an honest target public key, rather than the padding
itself. Standard BGV pseudorandomness hides this fixed offset.
     Our HRA proof is direct. Instead of first proving a stand-alone re-encryption
simulatability notion, we work inside the HRA game and preserve the public
consistency between visible honest-to-honest re-encryption keys and their out-
puts. The theorem is restricted to one re-encryption hop. After an honest-to-
honest hop, the inherited effective noise also contains key-switching and zero-
encryption-shield errors depending on the honest intermediate secret. If such a
ciphertext is later re-encrypted to a corrupted target, this effective noise may
itself become part of the leakage. Handling this would require an additional leak-
age theorem for BGV effective errors or a different refresh mechanism; we return
to this limitation in Section 4.

1.3   Related Work
Early lattice-based PRE constructions focused mainly on efficient delegation
and IND-CPA security. Polyakov, Rohloff, Sahu, and Vaikuntanathan [PRSV17]
used key-switching techniques to build efficient lattice-based PRE, while Co-
hen [Coh19] later showed that IND-CPA security alone is insufficient for PRE
because honest re-encryption transcripts may leak information about the re-
encryption process. This motivated the study of security against honest re-
encryption attacks.
    Existing HRA-secure lattice PRE constructions typically obtain re-encryption
simulatability through statistical smudging or flooding. Cohen, Cousins, Genise,
Kline, Polyakov, and Rv [CCG+ 25] give a tightly analysed RLWE-based HRA-
secure PRE construction using calibrated flooding. Related large-noise masking
mechanisms also appear in broader PRE settings, including the source-hiding ap-
proach of Fuchsbauer, Kamath, Klein, and Pietrzak [FKKP19], the strong blur-
ring construction of Chandran, Chase, Liu, Nishimaki, and Xagawa [CCL+ 14],

the unbounded multi-hop construction of Wan, Wang, Xue, and Wang [WWXW25],
and the fine-grained multi-hop schemes of Zhou, Liu, and Han [ZLH24]. These
works differ in functionality, but their HRA mechanisms rely on statistical hiding
rather than on computational error-leakage masking.
    Our work is also related to leakage-resilient variants of LWE. Lai, Swarnakar,
and Woo [LSW25] introduced the Leaky-LWE framework, which studies LWE
hardness in the presence of auxiliary leakage on the secret and error terms. The
NEL-LWE condition used in this paper is the error-only leakage case, instanti-
ated with leakage ℓ = e + epad .


1.4     Organisation

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the nec-
essary preliminaries, notation, and security notions. Section 3 presents the pro-
posed OE-PRE construction, introduces the NEL-LWE-based security frame-
work, and establishes correctness and single-hop HRA security by a direct HRA
hybrid. Section 3.4 compares the HRA-specific noise requirements with flooding-
based approaches. Section 4 gives a bounded multi-hop correctness analysis and
discusses the additional obstacle to multi-hop HRA security. Section 5 discusses
the application scope and future parameter-design directions. Section 6 concludes
the paper.

2.3     Owner-Encrypted Proxy Re-Encryption

Unlike standard public-key PRE, owner-encrypted proxy re-encryption (OE-
PRE) does not allow arbitrary third parties to encrypt messages under the dele-
gator’s public key. Instead, the delegator generates the initial ciphertext herself
using her secret key and later delegates decryption rights through a re-encryption
key.

Definition 4 (Owner-Encrypted Proxy Re-Encryption). An owner-encrypted
proxy re-encryption scheme OE-PRE consists of the following PPT algorithms.

    – Setup(1λ ) → pp. The setup algorithm outputs public parameters pp.
    – ProxyInit(pp) → stP = κpad . The proxy initialises its inner state.
    – KeyGen(pp) → (pk, sk). The key-generation algorithm outputs a public key
      and a secret key.
    – ReKeyGen(pp, pkA , skA , pkB ) → rkA→B . Given the delegator’s public and se-
      cret keys (pkA , skA ) and the delegatee’s public key pkB , the algorithm outputs
      a re-encryption key rkA→B . The delegatee’s secret key is not required.
    – Enc(pp, skA , m) → ctA . The owner-encryption algorithm takes the delegator’s
      secret key skA and a message m ∈ M, and outputs an owner-generated
      ciphertext ctA .

   a re-encryption key and a ciphertext under the delegator’s key domain, and

 – Dec(pp, sk, ct) → m or ⊥. The decryption algorithm takes a secret key and

Remark 2 (Proxy initialisation). The proxy may maintain local state across re-
encryption queries. While PRE servers typically store re-encryption keys and
access-control metadata, our construction also uses proxy-local state explicitly
to ensure deterministic reuse of the padding value for each source ciphertext.

Correctness. The single-hop correctness notion requires that decrypting a ci-

whelming probability. Since the security theorem proved in this work is single-
hop, the detailed iterative L-hop correctness definition is deferred to Section 4,
where we analyse bounded iteration only at the level of correctness.


2.4   Security for OE-PRE

We define single-hop IND-CPA and HRA security for OE-PRE by adapting the
standard HRA game [AFGH06,Coh19,FKKP19] to the owner-encrypted setting.
The game maintains a set Deriv that contains the challenge ciphertext and all
ciphertexts obtained from it via admissible re-encryption. The main difference
is that honest encryption uses the owner’s secret key.
    We use a selective-key formulation. All honest and corrupted users are cre-
ated before the challenge phase, and the corruption status of each user is fixed
throughout the experiment. Adaptive post-challenge key generation and adap-
tive corruptions are left outside the present model.

subsection, “single-hop” means that re-encryption queries are applied only to ci-

5     Discussion: Application Scope and Future Directions

5.1   Application Scope

The proved construction targets single-hop access delegation for owner-generated
ciphertexts. This is narrower than general public-key PRE, because only the data
owner generates the initial ciphertext, and narrower than general multi-hop PRE,
because our HRA theorem covers only one re-encryption hop. It nevertheless cap-
tures a common access-control pattern: a data owner encrypts an object before
outsourcing it, and a storage server or broker later transforms that ciphertext
once for an authorised recipient. Encrypted file sharing and storage [AFGH06]
and publish/subscribe delivery [PRSV17] are natural examples.
    The construction should not be read as a replacement for PRE systems that
require arbitrary public encryption or HRA-secure multi-hop routing. Its purpose
is to isolate the owner-generated single-hop delegation step and show that the
inherited-noise leakage in this step can be handled by computational masking
rather than by statistical flooding.


5.2   Future Parameter Design and Hybrid Multi-hop Extension

A concrete parameter design should choose d, q, p, Bg , σe , σpad jointly so that the
NEL-LWE condition of Corollary 1, the correctness bound of Theorem 1, and the
ordinary BGV pseudorandomness requirements hold simultaneously. It should
then estimate concrete LWE/RLWE security and compare ciphertext size, re-
encryption-key size, noise budget, and re-encryption cost with flooding-based
HRA-secure PRE.
    A second direction is a hybrid computational/statistical multi-hop design.
The first owner-generated hop could use NEL-LWE padding to avoid the initial
large flooding term, while later hops in a longer lineage could use calibrated
flooding, possibly combined with modulus switching and more precise noise ac-
counting [CCG+ 25, Ogi26]. Whether this can yield smaller later flooding widths
requires a separate parameter analysis and is left for future work.

6    Conclusion

We presented a BGV-style owner-encrypted proxy re-encryption construction
that achieves single-hop HRA security without statistical noise flooding. The
construction combines deterministic per-ciphertext padding with a fresh target-
key zero-encryption shield. The padding masks the inherited owner-encryption
error in honest-to-corrupted re-encryption queries, while the shield prevents the
fixed padding from being publicly extracted in visible honest-to-honest tran-
scripts.
    The security proof is a direct HRA hybrid. Its core step uses NEL-LWE
to handle the noisy leakage ect + epad , and the required NEL-LWE condition
follows from the Leaky-LWE framework under suitable parameters. The result-
ing security claim is based on standard LWE/RLWE-style pseudorandomness
assumptions, the NEL-LWE consequence of Leaky-LWE, and PRF security.
    We also analysed bounded iteration at the level of correctness and identified
the obstacle to multi-hop HRA security: after an honest-to-honest hop, the in-
herited effective noise contains key-switching and zero-encryption-shield errors
depending on the honest intermediate secret. Extending HRA security beyond
one hop without statistical flooding appears to require a new leakage-resilience
theorem for BGV effective errors, a stronger effective-error-leakage assumption,
or a hybrid computational/statistical refresh mechanism.
